#820. Oliver Hudson's Son Wilder Deferring College Due to "So Much Stress"

Oliver Hudson shared why his son Wilder is deferring his second semester of college, noting the teenager wanted to combat depression experiencing "so much stress" on campus.

Wilder Hudson has a new chapter on the books.

After all, his dad Oliver Hudson detailed how the 19-year-old—shared with actress Erinn Bartlett—dealt with depression on campus after a complicated wisdom teeth removal at home, ultimately leading him to take a break from college life.

"Going back to school was a bit of a task," Oliver said on his and sister Kate Hudson's Sibling Revelry podcast Nov. 6, explaining that after six weeks of dental issues, Wilder "felt a little depressed, like he didn’t belong there anymore."

According to the Grown-Ups 2 actor, the "false start" at the University of Colorado: Boulder caused his son to start "carrying so much stress.”

"Stress is a killer," the 50-year-old continued. "I'd rather you smoke a f--king pack of cigarettes than be stressed."

And after Wilder starred alongside his dad and Alicia Silverstone in Netflix's A Merry Little Ex-Mas, Oliver understood why his eldest felt he would be happier pursuing acting now since "college will still be there waiting for him."

As such, Oliver—also dad to Bodhi, 16, and Rio, 13, with Erinn—helped Wilder come up with the plan to defer his second semester and return to school for sophomore year.

"He wants to take a shot at his life, which means that, of course, he’ll still be living at home," Oliver clarified, "but he’s getting a job. He’s going to work on his auditions."

In addition, the upcoming actor will take a screenwriting class at a local community college to hone his craft because, while Oliver admitted nepotism "will get your foot in the door, no doubt about it," he's also learned that connections can't replace the ability to perform.

Keep reading for other stars speaking out about their mental health journeys.

The Grammy winner has been very open about how she protects her energy, such as ignoring haters on social media, while also sharing her advice for those who may need help.

"When people ask me what I'd say to somebody looking for advice on mental health, the only thing I can say is patience," she told Vogue. "I had patience with myself. I didn't take that last step. I waited. Things fade."

The Frozen star has talked for years about her strategies for coping with her mental health at public keynotes and even on her Instagram Stories.

She has advocated for finding the methods that help you best, which for her, according to Health, can include medication, listing ten positive things in her life for every negative thought and getting plenty of exercise.

While everyone was trying to make the best of socially distancing to slow the coronavirus pandemic, the "Firework" artist got real about how situations like this can also be extremely stressful.

"Sometimes I don't know what's worse trying to avoid the virus or the waves of depression that come with this new norm," she shared on Twitter. Katy talked about how she manages those waves, writing, "There is not really anywhere to go besides my car. So I go to my car a lot. That is my safe space."

The model, who teamed up with designer Kenneth Cole to raise awareness for The Mental Health Coalition, spoke on Good Morning America about her own experiences with anxiety.

She recalled after her panic attacks started recurring, she, "finally kind of got the information that I needed about it."

"For me, I have good days and I have some really anxious days, so I'm really off and on," Kendall expressed, adding that was why she wanted to become involved with the movement. "What I hope to accomplish is for people to not feel as alone."

The rapper (real name Radric Davis) revealed in his October 2025 book Episodes: The Diary of a Recovering Mad Man that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which prompted a mental health episode in 2020.

“After that, I was like, ‘Man, I got to really just hold myself accountable and take care of my health,’” he said on an episode of The Breakfast Club. “I don’t never want to have an episode again. I’m gonna see a therapist, [even] if I have to take medicine.”

In addition to his hope that his vulnerability would help others in need, Gucci Mane said that his kids Ice Davis and Iceland Ka’oir Davis with wife Keyshia Ka’Oir inspired him to seek help amid his episode.

“My wife was pregnant with my little boy,” he continued. “I don’t want to raise a family and then my mental health [is] gone. What if I have an episode I can’t come back from? So, I just started doing the work and started seeking help.”

In October 2026, the daughter of Teresa Giudice and Joe Giudice shared she was getting treatment for bipolar disorder in a candid update about her mental health journey.

"I do struggle with mental health issues," Milania told followers in an Oct. 12 Instagram video. "I am bipolar. I struggle with depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD and I am not ashamed of any of my mental health disorders because I'm currently at a treatment center, my mom's on her way to come visit me today."

The then-20-year-old added that "this summer hit me like a bus" after Milania was arrested for assault in May and her best friend Victoria Zardoya died suddenly in July.

"A lot of things happened in a short amount of time and I'm trying to just process everything," the University of Tampa student noted. "It's really hard being in the public light while you go through things in life."

The Gossip Girl alum detailed his experience as a child actor with what he described as "body dysmorphia."

“I know that I hated my body,” Penn told The Guardian in April 2025, “and simply wanted a different one.”

In response to the weight he gained following his parents' divorce, he added,  “There was just a period where, coming out of depression and isolation, I was jumping wilfully into, but also being thrust into, this world where the more conventionally beautiful I seemed, the more successful I might be, the more value I might have.”

Despite the mental struggles, though, Penn credited his ability to persist to his spirituality.

“That is what allowed me to persevere through the disillusionment, all the things I’d been grappling with,” he explained, “and then come back to it all, but with hopefully some kind of inner transformation.”

The Scrubs alum has been vocal about her past difficult relationship with food.

“Some may call it an eating disorder, I just call it my life,” she said on the The Funny Thing Is podcast. “My drug of choice was always food. I did crazy s--t with it.”

She added, “I would over-exercise, and there was a sprinkle of bulimia in there.”

Though she has confessed her struggles with her diet, she has also shared her progress with her health and fitness goals.

“When I was 23, I cut all sugar out of my diet, quit drinking, and found yoga and breathing and stretching,” she told Bon Appétit in 2017. “That’s the best Ritalin you could give anyone."

She continued, "I’m an actress with food issues and body image issues—that's real. But I'm trying to heal that part of myself and also handle my physical issues naturally by putting the best things into my body."

The Full House alum reflected on her mental health journey and navigating her battle with depression.

"It's very difficult to speak out about it, even to your most trusted people," she shared on her Candace Cameron Bure Podcast. "At least for me, I feel like I should be strong enough to overcome that and then it feels so weak."

The Black Adam actor has been open about having depression and how it can be difficult for men to talk about their mental health.

"We all go thru the sludge/shit and depression never discriminates. Took me a long time to realize it but the key is to not be afraid to open up," he wrote on Twitter. "Especially us dudes have a tendency to keep it in. You're not alone."

The Duke of Sussex helped break down some of the stigma around seeking help for mental health when, in an interview with the Telegraph, he opened up about his own journey with therapy. As he told the outlet, "The experience I have had is that once you start talking about it, you realize that actually you're part of quite a big club."

Another proponent of seeking professional help, the Empire star has been open about her struggles with depression."I have a therapist that I speak to," she previously told Variety. "That's the only way I can get through it."

Taraji even started The Boris Lawrence Henson Foundation, which works to reduce the stigma around mental health in the African American community and also works to increase the number of Black therapists.

The Grammy winner explained that experiences with an eating disorder and stage freight led her to start a form of PTSD treatment called MDMA and and psilocybin therapy.

“I was touring without stage fright for the first time,” she told Rolling Stone in May 2025. “There was a hook around my guts and everyone in the room was having the same feeling, [like] there’d been a huge pressure change. It made me realize how much I love and kind of need that very deep, visceral response to feel my music.”

She added that her renewed focus on her mental health, as well as her decision to stop taking birth control, caused her understanding of her own gender to become “more expansive.”

“I felt like stopping taking my birth control, I had cut some sort of cord between myself and this regulated femininity,” she continued. “It sounds crazy, but I felt that all of a sudden, I was off the map of femininity. And I totally believed that that allowed things to open up.”

"When I was in middle school, I was struggling with severe anxiety and depression and the help and support I received from my family and a therapist saved my life," the Riverdale actress wrote on Instagram in 2017.  "Asking for help is the first step. You are more precious to this world than you'll ever know."

The “What He Didn’t Do” singer shared insight into what her life has been like during her yearslong battle with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

“I would have told you three years ago my anxiety started during my divorce in Covid,” Carly said an August 2025 episode of Bunnie Xo’s Dumb Blonde podcast. “But I’ve had crippling OCD since I was a child.”

“I got really conditioned over the last 10 years to just zip it up and deal with it, and it just kind of got to a place where a couple years ago I just had to really start back into therapy, start really, like, trying to figure out all of these different things,” she continued. “Like, recognizing OCD was something—no, that didn’t come in 2020, that’s been there since I was 6 or 7.”

While the cookbook author is the proud parent to four kiddos, she's also been open about postpartum depression that many new mothers experience but feel like they cannot talk about.

"It got easier and easier to say it aloud every time," she wrote in an open letter to Glamour in 2017. "I want people to know it can happen to anybody and I don't want people who have it to feel embarrassed or to feel alone."

While promoting her book Mirror, Mirror, the model opened up to The Edit magazine about facing depression and suicidal thoughts as a teenager, saying she felt "something dark" in her during that time.

"I relied too much on love, too much on other people to make me happy, and I needed to learn to be happy by myself," Cara told the publication, via W. "So now I can be by myself, I can be happy. It took me a long time."

The "Thank U, Next" artist has encouraged fans to seek help if they need, responding to a Twitter user who joked about wondering who Ariana's therapist is with, "lmaoaoo this is funny as f--k but in all honesty therapy has saved my life so many times."

"If you're afraid to ask for help, don't be," she continued. "u don't have to be in constant pain & u can process trauma. I've got a lot of work to do but it's a start to even be aware that it's possible."

The singer has been open about her journey with addiction, sobriety, mental health and more, including many of those aspects of her life within her music.

She also continually reminds fans that working on your mental health is an ongoing process where there will be some bad days, previously writing on Instagram, "A reminder to anyone struggling out there - this life is a journey with tons of ups and downs but you can't give up."

Not only has the actress taken on roles that deal with mental health, such as her role as Rue in the teen drama Euphoria, she's also addressed those issues in her own life, too.

Back in 2013, Zendaya wrote on her now-defunct app that she struggled with anxiety after an appearance on Ellen where her mic went out. She has since learned ways to manage those feelings, adding, "Sometimes you just have to take a step back so things stop stressin' you."

The singer candidly described her mental health journey with WSJ Magazine, saying, "My highs were really high, and my lows would take me out for weeks at a time."

"I found out I do suffer from mental health issues," she shared. "I got on the right medication, and my life has been completely changed."

The Grammy winner made it her mission to spread kindness and be open about mental health, including her own.

"I have struggled for a long time, both being public and not public about my mental health issues or my mental illness," she said during the Global Changemakers Award at Children Mending Hearts' Empathy Rocks fundraiser in 2018. "But, I truly believe that secrets keep you sick."

#819. Is there something missing despite Rangers' impressive form?

Rangers have won 10 and drawn two of their past 12 matches in all competitions

Rangers are unbeaten in their past 12 matches in all competitions, winning 10 of them, and moved to within a point of the Scottish Premiership summit after Saturday's 2-0 win away to St Mirren.

They thoroughly deserved their victory. They have the best defensive record in the top flight and the third best attacking record, but it feels as though they are not playing to their full potential.

In Paisley, Derek McInnes' side never quite put the game to bed despite a host of chances and St Mirren should really have pulled one back in the closing stages.

"There's still not that element of control," former Celtic striker Chris Sutton said on Sky Sports.

"That killer instinct is really important, but they don't control games the way they should. That will be the worry. Eventually that will bite Rangers in the backside."

Sutton's sparring partner on Sky - former Rangers and Scotland striker Kris Boyd - agreed.

"They are a good team, but with Rangers teams of the past, that would have been three or four," he said.

Rangers overcome St Mirren to move point behind Celtic

Ryan Naderi - who put Rangers in front from the penalty spot and has scored six in his past eight league matches - should have scored before he did.

Strike partner Kevin Kelsy missed a host of chances at the start of the second half before midfielder Dan Neil's deflected shot nestled in the bottom corner to make it 2-0.

Rangers' expected goals in their 12 league matches this season is 29.8. They have scored just 21.

Key striking duo Youssef Chermiti and Lawrence Shankland are both out injured and that goes some way to explaining their profligacy in front of goal, but it doesn't tell the full story.

Naderi and Kelsy have performed admirably this season - there have only been two matches since August in which neither man has scored.

It is the players behind them who have not fully stepped up to the plate.

South Korean winger Kim Min-su is yet to score or assist in Rangers colours since signing from Girona in the summer, although he created more chances than any other player on Saturday, while Badredine Bouanani has shown undoubted quality without regularly delivering end product.

Against St Mirren, there were plenty of promising attacking positions that did not result in a shot as players took the wrong option and allowed the home defence to recover.

As McInnes pointed out: "Loads of chances. It's quite ironic we scored from a penalty and a deflected shot, but some of our work was really clean up until the last part.

"What becomes a good chance could be a brilliant chance if we just take care with the weight of pass and make the right decision.

"There are umpteen examples in that game today and it's something we need to improve on. We've got to take ownership that we can do better in these moments.

"The top players make these decisions at breakneck speed and pick the right pass."

It is obviously something McInnes has impressed on his players and Neil referenced the need to be more ruthless.

"We speak all the time about being more clinical and there were a couple of chances we could have done better with," the former Sunderland midfielder said.

McInnes - who fell agonisingly short of winning the title with Heart of Midlothian last season - was open about how he wants and expects more from his players moving forwards, despite their impressive form.

"It's not been perfect," he said of the past two and a half months. "We've had the draw with Hearts and the draw at Dundee.

"Our fight is with ourselves to keep improving. If we can keep winning and getting those improvements as we go along, there's hopefully more to come from us."

If those improvements do come, Sutton believes Rangers could be hard to stop.

"They seem like a team that have another gear or two and that will be a worry for the other teams in the league," he added.

#817. Dalot’s muddled performances are just another symptom of Old Trafford chaos | Will Unwin

The stand-in left-back has become a pantomime villain but United fans are understandably struggling to focus their ire

Sporting success is, supposedly, a nigh-on irrelevance to Manchester United’s global brand. The money will stream in regardless thanks to the behemoth company it has become, leaving behind its football club roots and becoming the world’s greatest soap opera creating the sort of drama of which Phil Mitchell can only dream.

There is a strong cast of characters from the hated billionaire owners to the under‑pressure manager and pantomime villain Diogo Dalot, and a collection of storylines that are becoming hard to believe. Amid the supervillains, there are the unmistakable petty culprits who have brought United down to 18th place in the Premier League and Michael Carrick wondering how much longer he can survive.

Within four minutes, United were two goals behind and wondering if they could perform another miracle as they did against Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday. Compared with the start of the season, there is more fight and anger in this team, inspired by Matheus Cunha, a player who can match talent with desire. It was a fine collective performance from conceding the second until the break, admittedly with Dalot being caught out to allow Alysson through on goal, only to nudge wide on the verge of half‑time.

Dalot is part of the problem, an unwitting victim of circumstances, mainly that he is a disappointing right‑back being forced to play out of position because no one saw fit to find a backup for the injury‑prone Luke Shaw at left‑back. The director of football, Jason Wilcox, was targeted by supporters’ chants, suggesting that he leave the club with rather fruity language because he is a key reason that Dalot is bumbling along in a defence that has conceded 30 goals already in all competitions – the joint-most of any side in Europe’s top five leagues.

The Portugal international has been at Old Trafford for more than eight years but it is an overstayed welcome because he is not good enough. Every match involves him committing more and more petty footballing crimes that are adding up to a long charge sheet for someone who claims to be an experienced defender. He is so often found out of position, a first-time observer could think he is playing left-wing or central midfield.

Against Roma he was at least partly culpable for the Italian side’s two goals because he had lost his bearings. United got away with it that night and were given the chance to rectify the tactics and Dalot’s understanding of what a full-back should do, instead of acting as a catalyst for chaos that United could do without. Within a minute, however, he was confused about whether to go towards Alysson on the edge of the box or leave the Brazilian to his own devices. He chose the latter option, allowing the winger to get a shot away and through Senne Lammens’ legs for another dreadful mistake.

The 20-year-old Alysson arrived in the country in January but already looks a settled Premier League talent, and had the better of Dalot for the entire time the two were on the pitch.

Getting to 2-2 was an achievement and United were in the ascendancy but returned without Harry Maguire for the second half, putting greater responsibility on the shoulders of Dalot, who now had Ayden Heaven beside him. Dalot has 40 caps for one of Europe’s best national teams but none of that was evident when he tripped Alysson inside the box, allowing John McGinn to swing the momentum in Villa’s favour.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Dalot lasted until the 66th minute when Carrick had seen enough, getting his ejection held aloft in red. At least with the new rules, Dalot was forced to jog off within 10 seconds to speed up his exit after a disastrous day’s work. The United fans cheered when it was clear he was being substituted, preferring Patrick Dorgu. It was a rather underwhelming changing of the guard but everyone has had enough of the Red Devil they know.

Elsewhere, Dalot’s form would have led to him being dropped for repeated poor performances but United do not possess serious squad depth. They have won once in 10 league matches to leave them deservedly in the relegation zone after more than a quarter of the season. Dalot is a symptom of United’s chronic problems, with the simple truth that despite the results being appalling, no one on the bench, apart from the teenager Shea Lacey, is challenging for a starting berth.

No one likes to see an individual be the focal point of criticism for tens of thousands, especially as Dalot is merely a scapegoat. He shouldn’t be at left‑back or still even at the club because he has shown himself to be below par for far too long but there is a lack of cut-throat behaviour to rid themselves of the ineffectual. Without Dalot’s ineptitude, life this week would have been considerably easier for United. Of course, there were celebrations at full-time after another dramatic comeback but it was not a win on any level.

#816. Failed to deal with Brobbey - player ratings for Sunderland v Chelsea

Brobbey won the penalty in Sunderland's second league win of the season

Enzo Le Fee's penalty proved the difference as Sunderland climbed off the bottom of the table with a win over Chelsea.

Chelsea defender Levi Colwill brought down Brian Brobbey in the 36th minute, with Le Fee sending goalkeeper Mike Penders the wrong way from the spot.

Here is how I rated the players and how you rated them.

Sunderland beat Chelsea for first league win since August

Robin Roefs: The Dutch goalkeeper was rarely tested but dealt comfortably with the attempts that came his way. 7

Thomas Meunier: A solid and disciplined display at full-back while marking danger man Morgan Rogers. The Belgian also produced a superb tackle in the box midway through the second half. 8

Nordi Mukiele: The returning defender was a huge presence at the back, combining physicality with composure. 7

Luke O'Nien: The defender was fortunate not to concede a penalty after making contact with Cole Palmer but VAR judged it to be just outside the box. He also tested the Chelsea goal early in the second half. 6

Reinildo Mandava: It was a busy afternoon for the full-back, who was heavily tested down his flank by different big-name attackers. 7

Trai Hume: Hume saw a well-struck left-footed volley blocked in the opening moments of the game, while his defensive work was typically diligent throughout. 7

Noah Sadiki: Produced a disciplined display, filling gaps in midfield and frustrating Chelsea's attackers. 7

Granit Xhaka: The Sunderland captain went off injured after less than three minutes. N/A

Enzo Le Fee: The Frenchman's penalty sent Mike Penders the wrong way and proved the difference. 7

Chemsdine Talbi: Produced a wonderful cross in the 15th minute to create a chance for Brian Brobbey and played an important role linking defence and attack on the counter. 7

Brian Brobbey: A powerful presence up front. An early effort was scuffed wide, but he grew into the game and dominated Levi Colwill in several aerial duels. He came close to a brilliant solo goal before winning the penalty. 8

Jules Ahoka (on 4, Xhaka): Booked shortly after coming on but played well despite being on a yellow card and was key in winning the ball in midfield. 7

Wilson Isador (on 67, Brobbey): A tough ask following Brobbey and missed a big chance late on but showed his energy to help his team over the line. 6

Subs not used: Ellborg, Danso, Methalie, Tutierov, Fofana

Mike Penders: There was talk of number one Emiliano Martinez returning, but the young number two kept his place. The Belgian was sent the wrong way for the penalty and could do little to prevent the goal, but made a great save from Isador to keep it at 1-0. 6

Marco Palestra: Having suffered injury setbacks and still appearing to adapt to the league, the young Italian put in a positive attacking display and could have earned an assist with a cross midway through the first half. 6

Wesley Fofana: A stable performance after a shaky one last week at home to Manchester United. 6

Levi Colwill: Had a difficult afternoon and failed to deal with Brian Brobbey, who caught him out for a chance midway through the half before winning the penalty. Although it appeared a harsh decision, Colwill could have handled the situation better. He was then taken off at half-time having also been booked. 4

Pep Chavarria: An excellent early block prevented what looked a near-certain goal. He also delivered a dangerous cross, but nobody attacked it. 6

Moises Caicedo: Largely anonymous in midfield before moving to become a makeshift centre-back in the second half. 5

Romeo Lavia: Operated as a deep-lying playmaker but saw a long-range effort fail to trouble the goalkeeper. 6

Jordan Henderson: Returned to the starting line-up in a decent but unremarkable display at his former club. 5

Cole Palmer: Palmer's brilliant first touch and drive into the penalty area could have won a spot-kick when he was brought down by Luke O'Nien, but the incident was deemed to have taken place outside the box. 6

Morgan Rogers: Headed a good opportunity wide midway through the first half and was largely peripheral. 5

Pedro Neto: Neto was ineffective up front and taken off in the 62nd minute. 5

Estevao Willian (on 46, Colwill): The Brazilian showed threat after coming on. 6

Danny Welbeck (on 62, Neto): Added presence in the box, highlighted by a glancing header going wide moments after coming on. 6

Malo Gusto (on 62, Palestra): A quiet display in his 100th Premier League appearance. 6

Subs not used: Sharman-Lowe, Anselmino, Nicoll-Jazuli, Barco

Wirtz scored his first Premier League goal of the season

Liverpool win at Palace to pile pressure on Sage

#814. Enzo Maresca rues Manchester City’s lack of desire after defeat at Nottingham Forest

‘You need desire and intensity … we didn’t match them’

City have now lost three successive league matches

Enzo Maresca blamed his side’s lack of desire and the way they were outgunned in duels for a third successive Premier League defeat. After winning their first seven games of the season, Manchester City’s 3-1 loss at Nottingham Forest extended their poor run.

Jair Cunha dispossessed Josko Gvardiol to score the opener, then Liam Delap struck twice with muscular surges on the break as Forest won their first home league game since April. “Today I think [the problem] has been general,” said Maresca. “It’s not about one player. In the first half we lost all the duels, all the contacts. Against this team, that is fighting relegation, if you don’t match them … it’s something we need to understand. In this kind of game, if you’re not able to win duels and second balls like in the first half, you struggle.

“You need desire and intensity to win second balls and duels. You require intensity or you struggle and we didn’t match their intensity. The second and third goals are copy and paste, lost duels first in the middle of pitch then at the edge of the box.”

City’s 100% record came to an end with a 2-1 defeat away by Aston Villa, and they followed that up last week with a 1-0 home reverse against Brighton. “They are all different,” said Maresca. “But if you look at chances, possession, chances inside box, in all of them we were much, much better but we lost all of them. We’re going to use this international break to clarify what we can do better. We know we need to improve things and avoid this kind of game.”

After his frustrated reaction to last week’s defeat at Brentford, Oliver Glasner was understandably delighted that his reset, ending what he had referred to as compromises, had paid off.

“The way we play football I think we’ve had many better games,” he said. “But how we defended, how passionately we defended, how tactically smart we defended, it was one of our better games.

“You should control everything and if you want to control it, you have to run because you have to be so quickly aware – they’re so good, such great players, such a good structure and they move the ball so quickly. Of course, you can just defend but you also need to go forward and this is what we did today in the right moments.”

#813. European Central Bank (ECB) head Christine Lagarde to step down in February, before her term ends

European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde is to resign nine months ahead of the end of her 8-year term. European Council President Antonio Costa has said the process to find a successor is underway.

Christine Lagarde, who has headed the European Central Bank for seven years, has announced that she is stepping down prematurely from the position.

"European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on 7 February 2027," the ECB said in a statement.

European Council President Antonio Costa said a process to find her successor would start immediately.

The announcement comes ahead of a key meeting of the bank this week that is likely to focus on France's deteriorating public finances.

No reason has so far been given for Lagarde's premature departure, but there has been speculation that she would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose her successor before French elections in the spring that could see a eurosceptic far-right victory influence the choice.

Her term, which began on November 1, 2019, would normally have ended at the end of October 2027.

Lagarde, a former French finance minister, was also head of the International Monetary Fund from 2011 to 2019.

Costa praised Lagarde's leadership during her seven-year stint at the ECB helm, a period in which the EU and the world faced great challenges.

"Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area," Costa posted on social media.

"To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision," Costa said.

Lagarde herself has voiced satisfaction with her record.

"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde, a French economist, said in a short video shared on ​social media.

The ECB head is chosen by the leaders of the 21 eurozone countries.

The announcement of Lagarde's imminent departure comes as the ECB is to hold a meeting this week where it is expected to keep its ​deposit rate at 2.5%, while signaling that this is likely to rise again before the end of the year.

The bank has already raised interest rates twice since June in a bid to curb inflation fueled by the energy shock caused by the Iran war.

However, Thursday's meeting is also likely to focus on the fiscal and political crisis in France, Europe's second-biggest economy.

French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, rose to their highest level in 25 years last week amid a deadlock over next year's budget.

Recent protests, at which many demonstrators were calling for more spending on public services, were also marred by considerable violence.

There has been speculation as to whether the ECB could, for the first time, use the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI),  a crisis-fighting tool that allows the bank to buy bonds of a eurozone member if yields rise uncontrollably and there is a risk of financial stress spreading.

However, most observers believe the problems in France do not yet meet the strict conditions stipulated for its use.

#812. Chengdu blow 12-point lead to miss out on Chinese title on final day

Chengdu lost 1-0 to Dalian in their penultimate game of the season

Chengdu Rongcheng lost a fourth successive game to give up a 12-point lead and throw away the Chinese Super League title.

A 3-2 loss on the final day to Shandong Taishan, combined with a 3-1 win for Dalian Yingbo against Tianjin Tiger, meant John Aloisi's side missed out on the Li Guozu trophy.

It was a remarkable finale for Chengdu, who picked up just one point from their last five matches, while Dalian collected 15 from 15.

Both sides finished level on 52 points, but Dalian took the title with a better head-to-head record which included a victory over Chengdu in the penultimate game of the season.

The title-race collapse will go down as one of the worst in football history, especially with the faltering finish from the side led by Australian Aloisi, who had spells at Portsmouth and Coventry City during his playing career.

Kevin Keegan's Newcastle United famously gave up a 12-point lead to Manchester United in 1995-96 to miss out on the Premier League, while the Red Devils also blew a 12-point advantage over Arsenal in the 1997-98 campaign.

Despite their dreadful run of form, the title was still very much in Chengdu's hands going into the final day.

A point would have been enough to crown them champions, but they found themselves 2-0 down within the opening 25 minutes as Raphael Merkies and Guilherme Madruga scored.

Felipe Silva replied, but Cryzan restored Shandong's two-goal lead.

Former Arsenal forward Wellington Silva gave Aloisi's side hope again with 11 minutes left, but they were unable to find the all-important equaliser.

That outcome left Dalian needing a win in front of their own fans to secure a remarkable title triumph.

They were in front inside five minutes through Yang Mingrui, but Xadas levelled with a 50th-minute penalty.

Liao Jintao, though, restored the lead with 20 minutes to go before a close-range strike from Huang Shan in stoppage time sealed the success and the title.

#811. Evanilson ignites eighth straight Bournemouth win at blundering Ipswich

Marco Rose paid tribute to his Bournemouth side after a hard‑fought 2-1 victory at Ipswich equalled the club’s record of eight consecutive wins.

Evanilson got the ball rolling after five minutes, scoring for a fifth successive Premier League match. With seven goals this season, he has already beaten his tally from the whole of last season.

His latest was a gift from the Ipswich goalkeeper, Christian Walton, who tried and failed to dribble past ­him in the area, and Bournemouth went two up after 27 seconds of the second half when Leif Davis could only deflect Ryan Christie’s strike into his own net.

Lewis Cook tripped Abdoul ­Ouattara in the area to provide the hosts with a lifeline and Jack Clarke scored the penalty with 17 minutes left to set up a grandstand finish at Portman Road.

However, Bournemouth stood firm to make it eight wins in a row and match the record set under Eddie Howe in 2012-13, a season which ended with promotion from League One.

Speaking after a win which came three days after a victorious journey to Sparta Prague, Rose said: “I am pleased with the first 70 minutes because we went two up and I didn’t feel like we struggled or can get any problems, but it’s [the] Premier League and one goal changed the momentum of the game.

“That is why I am much more pleased with the last 20 minutes. We suffered but we did it together.”

A slow start last month at Chelsea proved costly for Bournemouth, and even in last weekend’s 2-0 home win against Leeds the visitors had an effort ruled out after 11 minutes. That made goals at the start of each half particularly sweet for Rose.

“Last week I said we start slow and this week I said we start quite quick and score an early goal. I am a magician!” the German said with a smile. “No, we know we have to be ready in this league. We played Chelsea four weeks ago and we were two down after three minutes. That’s why we learned and always good to score an early goal.

“We were sharp, we were good and that’s what I really appreciate. I said before this week that it’s going to be really demanding for a team that is not used to have this kind of [­European] situation.”

Julio Enciso went close late on with two free‑kicks, but this defeat means Ipswich have only won one of their last seven in all competitions.

Gary O’Neil, their manager, said: “[We are] gutted with the result, firstly, because it’s what we are here for and probably performance-wise not much in it. To lose a football match you’ve not been outclassed in is hard to take. But if you give the ball to the opposition No 9 twice, it’s going to be difficult and that was the story of the game really.

“It’s the level so we have to find a way of not only being competitive in games, but can we now find a way to make sure these Hull [a 2-2 draw] and Bournemouth performances are four points and not one.”

#810. Suki Waterhouse Teases Holiday Plans With Robert Pattinson & Daughter

Suki Waterhouse shared insight into how she and fiancé Robert Pattinson are celebrating the holidays with their daughter during an exclusive E! News interview at the 2026 CFDA Awards.

Suki Waterhouse is ready to sleigh this winter.

After all, the "Good Looking" singer revealed how she and fiancé Robert Pattinson plan to celebrate the holiday season with their 2-year-old daughter.

"The tradition I'm most looking forward to is just dressing the tree," Waterhouse exclusively told E! News at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards Presented by Amazon Fashion Nov. 2. "I'm really big into mulled wine. I'm excited to go back to London and start drinking a lot of mulled wine."

In fact, you can even call her a model, actress and winemaker.

"I will make my own mulled wine," she beamed. "I like it that much. It's dangerous how much I like mulled wine! I will be gifting my mulled wine."

Waterhouse and the Twilight star—who got engaged in December 2023 after five years of dating—are especially excited to celebrate the holiday season with their little spider monkey.

As she put it, "I go big at Christmas. I'm excited."

Though the couple is looking forward to breaking out the eggnog and blasting Christmas tunes, they're still learning how to navigate life as working parents.

"You're always finding the balance," the Daisy Jones & The Six alum admitted. "It's like you become a juggler, but we're all juggling. It feels good. I'm just having a great time with her."

And being a mom has made it so easy for the 34-year-old to love, to love, to love the most classic elements of her style.

"My staples are important, like great leather jackets," she explained. "You know me, I love my coats. I'm big into my coats, my boots, belts—just having the structure of an outfit there, and the day is good."

As for where she finds the inspo for her closet? Waterhouse traveled all the corners where destiny called her and it was in the '60s and '70s.

"My biggest fashion inspiration is probably people like Anita Pallenberg, Patti Smith, Pattie Boyd, Marianne Faithfull," she explained. "How it's translated to my own—I love boyish clothes, anything that, vintage sourcing, stuff like that."

While Waterhouse and Pattinson prepare for the coziest time of year, keep reading to see more of the actress' style during their sweetest moments.

Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson first sparked relationship speculation in July 2018, when they were photographed on a PDA-filled date night in London.

In Dec. 2022, the private pair made their relationship red carpet official at Dior's fashion show in Egypt...

...where they couldn't help but show off their love.

The Daisy Jones actress and the Twilight alum turned the 2023 Met Gala into a date night on the first Monday in May.

The couple attended GO Campaign's 17th annual GO Gala at Citizen News in Hollywood on Oct. 21.

About two weeks after Suki confirmed her pregnancy, she and Rob went to the Poor Things premiere in New York. And they weren't the only stars there as Taylor Swift was also at the event.

In February 2023, Suki shared rare insight into her relationship with Rob. "I'm always incredibly excited when I see his name pop up [on my phone] or even a text, and I think he feels the same about me," she told The Sunday Times. "We've always got so much to say, and I find him hilarious."

"Rob definitely isn't getting advice from me about acting," Suki shared with The Sunday Times, "but of course I'll try and get him to help me with an audition before he falls asleep on the sofa."

The singer introduced the couple's baby on Instagram April 4, writing, "welcome to the world angel."

The pair made their first official joint appearance since welcoming their daugher Oct. 5, 2024 at the Veuve Clicquot Polo Classic in Pacific Palisades, Calif.

#809. 'I can't believe he is one of us' - inside Salah's life in Trabzon

Mohamed Salah has scored 10 goals in 15 games for Turkish club Trabzonspor

Back in August, when Mohamed Salah landed in Istanbul after flying in from his holiday in Mykonos, he wore Trabzonspor's burgundy and blue home strip as he stepped out of the plane to be greeted by thousands of fans.

That kit sold out almost instantly. Later that day, as Salah headed to Trabzon in north-east Turkey to complete the formalities of one of the most unexpected transfers after the expiry of his Liverpool contract, he asked one of his entourage what he should wear.

"The same kit," came the response, but Trabzonspor president Ertugrul Dogan advised Salah to wear the black away kit instead. Of course, that sold out too.

From the outset of the 34-year-old's arrival to this historic port city on the Black Sea, that sense of adulation has only grown.

"I went to the airport to see him in Istanbul and it was surreal," says Nisa Dumangoz. "I still can't believe that he is one of us."

Go for a stroll through Trabzon on matchday and it is Salah's face which adorns everything. Even the walls inside the fishmongers have pictures of him.

At the club shop in town, one of the staff jokes that the ground floor is for the Egyptian and the upper floor is for everything else.

Outside the stadium, there are scarves, magnets, keyrings, lighters with his face on and Egyptian Nemes headdresses in Trabzonspor colours. Season ticket sales rocketed after his arrival.

"Walking around Trabzon, it feels as though nine out of every 10 fans wearing a shirt have Salah's name on the back. The 10th has their own," says Turkish football journalist Hasan Tuncel.

The club have surpassed their merchandise revenue from last year in three months since Salah's arrival, while the local airport is only getting busier.

Liverpool was difficult to reach for many supporters across the Arab world and tickets were often hard to source. Trabzon is far more accessible, with new flights introduced from Cairo, Dubai and Riyadh since Salah's arrival.

On our flight from Istanbul, we meet an Egyptian family of 10 coming from Cairo for Trabzonspor's Uefa Conference League game against Freiburg.

"He is our ambassador and our Egyptian King, and with how many people want to come to Turkey now, he is their ambassador too," says Mahmoud.

At the game, there is a group of Egyptian celebrities and influencers. A quick check of their social media shows their combined Instagram following of about five million. Trabzonspor have three million. Salah has 68 million.

Salah recently went for a hike and posed for a picture on a rock in the Trabzon highlands. That rock has been renamed Salahtasi (Salah's Rock) and is now a tourist destination.

The commercial element of his signing has more than been justified but crucially, on the pitch, Salah is driving Trabzonspor's push for the Turkish Super Lig title and he has hit the ground running with 10 goals and five assists in all competitions.

Trabzonspor trail leaders Galatasaray by three points, having won seven of their first 10 games, including victories against the table-toppers and Besiktas.

For context, the Istanbul 'big three' of Galatasaray (26), Fenerbahce (19) and Besiktas (16) have won the league on 61 occasions combined, compared with Trabzonspor's seven titles.

"In Turkey, he is the biggest football star after Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo," says Kerim Tonyali, who is part of Gurbetci Gencler, a Trabzonspor supporters' group.

And given Salah's status as an icon, Trabzonspor are quickly becoming the second club for many in Turkey and the wider Muslim world.

Salah's face is a common sight wherever you go in Trabzon

Trabzon may be more than 2,000 miles from Liverpool but there are similarities, particularly when it comes to the sense of identity and pride associated with originating from here.

"Everywhere is Trabzon for us," is the local mantra and aligns with the sense of unity within this city that has a population of about 800,000 and is only the 30th-biggest in Turkey.

For Salah, the financials were important and he is earning about Â£14.6m per year as well as 20% of official merchandise sold with his name on, but one of the key aspects of coming here was the ability to focus entirely on his football.

Besiktas was considered as an option after the 2026 World Cup but, after multiple calls with Trabzonspor, Salah felt they were the ideal fit and offered a life away from the hustle and bustle of Istanbul.

He has his own security detail and is living in the nearby town of Yomra, where he now has a street named after him. He also employs a private chef and, unsurprisingly, continues to set standards in the gym and on the training ground.

By all accounts, Salah is thriving. He is a fan of Turkish coffee and is often spotted leaving the ground with Ayran - a traditional yogurt drink - but as much as he wants to explore the city, he knows of the difficulties given his reputation.

"Everyone wants to work with a star like Mohamed Salah," said Trabzonspor's Paul Onuachu, formerly of Southampton. "He adds so much and helps all of us and he contributes positively. I am grateful for him. It's a blessing to play with him."

Watching Salah in the flesh in a Conference League game against Freiburg, his pace has gone down a notch compared with his peak but the touch, quick feet and sheer quality is still there. And so is that knack of getting in goalscoring positions, even if his defensive duties - which were such a source of debate last season at Liverpool - are limited.

Salah believes he still has plenty to give for club and country, with aspirations to play in both the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations and 2030 World Cup, which will be partly held in North Africa.

No decision has been made about how long he will stay in Turkey, but there is growing belief among sources in the Middle East that he will move to Saudi Arabia when his two-year Trabzonspor deal expires in 2028. By then, he will be 36.

Salah signed a two-year deal with Trabzonspor in the summer of 2026

On initial thoughts, it is easy to question how and why Salah ended up here.

When he delivered that infamous mixed-zone interview at Leeds' Elland Road less than a year ago and the wheels of his departure from Liverpool were set in motion, surely no-one would have imagined his next destination would be this Turkish outpost near the Georgian border.

"I remember looking at him when we landed in Trabzon and seeing the crowds outside and how emotional it was," says Anil Dincer, one of the lawyers involved in Salah's move to Turkey.

"We already have Salah and Fabinho. So now we are waiting for [Virgil] Van Dijk," adds Serhat Sumer, a Trabzonspor fan.

Salah, of course, delivered so much joy to Liverpool and the intention here is the same. This is no drift towards retirement, but a player determined to prove he still belongs at the highest level and that football still has meaning beyond trophies and money.

Asked by BBC Sport if he had a message for Liverpool fans, Salah simply said "hello" and smiled. Given how rarely he spoke in the mixed zone during his time at Anfield, it is not in his nature to talk regularly on record.

Last season was Salah's least prolific at Anfield, but given Liverpool's struggles in front of goal in the Premier League, it is hard to argue they have replaced one of their greatest ever players.

Perhaps a time will come when the likes of Salah, Arne Slot and Richard Hughes will reveal more about the chain of events that led to the forward agreeing to terminate his contract a year early. As it is, none of them are at the club and that chapter is firmly closed.

Salah's influence that once helped shape the Premier League is now being felt on the shores of the Black Sea. He is Trabzonspor's force of nature. And the team known as the Black Sea Storm are rising and on the hunt for silverware with their Egyptian King.

A rock in the Trabzon highlands became a tourist destination after Salah's visit

#808. FA Cup roundup: Seventh-tier Wimborne shock Crawley to reach second round

Grimsby and Stockport survive scares but Wednesday out

Exeter upset League One leaders Huddersfield

Seventh-tier Wimborne heaped more misery on Crawley as the bottom side in the Football League lost 2-0 in the biggest upset of the FA Cup first round.

The Dorset part-timers took the lead after only nine minutes when the property surveyor Yang Seung-woo curled a superb strike from just inside the penalty area into the top corner.

Crawley came close to equalising when Kai Jennings flashed a low shot narrowly wide before Jonny Russell headed tamely into the arms of the home goalkeeper Cam Plain.

Crawley’s interim manager, Kevin Blackwell, made a triple change at half-time and Charlie Barker fired inches wide for the team 57 places above their hosts in the pyramid. The Southern Premier League South side got a huge slice of luck to seal victory 11 minutes from time. Jackson King’s shot hit Cameron Munn to send the ball squirming beyond the former Arsenal goalkeeper Vito Mannone.

Will Sutton scored a dramatic extra-time winner for Oldham as Dave Challinor’s first game in charge of Sheffield Wednesday ended in an upset. The homegrown central defender was up for a free-kick which the Owls failed to clear, with Sutton left completely free to nod home from six yards and secure a 2-1 win.

Calum Kavanagh put Oldham ahead in the 66th minute with a fierce drive after Mike Fondop headed on Noah Chilvers’ right-wing cross. Wednesday equalised 10 minutes later through the former Oldham forward Davis Keillor-Dunn.

The match ignited further in the 84th minute following a touchline fracas involving a large number of players. The Oldham manager, Micky Mellon, was sent off and Sheffield Wednesday’s Callum Slattery was booked. After Sutton’s winning goal, Oldham defended resolutely to close out the game.

Stafford Rangers were denied a historic win after losing 3-2 on penalties to Grimsby after they drew 3-3 after extra time. Two goals from firefighter Darrhyl Mason and one from the Aston Villa youth coach Jack Birch got the eighth-tier side – 89 places below League Two Grimsby – to a shootout.

Mason and Birch had put Rangers 2-0 ahead in front of a crowd of 3,130 at the Stan Robinson Stadium as they chased the second round for the first time since 2007. But set-piece headers inside three minutes from Harvey Rodgers and Maldini Kacurri sent the tie into extra time, where Mason and Géza Turi traded goals.

The home debutant Luca Navarro had to score to send the tie into sudden death but saw his spot-kick saved by Harvey Cartwright to end Rangers’ nine-match Cup marathon.

Lewis Fiorini’s extra-time penalty sent Stockport, who are second in League One, into the second round after they came from two goals down with 10 men to win 3-2 against Cray Wanderers.

Despite being 112 places below their opponents in the pyramid, it was the Isthmian Premier side Cray who took the lead after 21 minutes when Sammie MacLeod found the bottom corner.

Stockport were then reduced to 10 men in the 31st minute as goalkeeper Luca Ashby-Hammond was sent off for a dangerous challenge on John Ufuah. Alex Hernández bent a brilliant strike into the top corner from the resulting free-kick.

Depleted Stockport pulled one back in the 81st minute when Kyle Wootton tscored with a header. And the Hatters then sent the tie into extra time when Mikael Mandron was in the right place to nod home Jack Diamond’s cross. The decisive moment came in the 101st minute when Cray goalkeeper JJ Briggs clattered into Mandron to give away a penalty, which was dispatched by Fiorini.

Charlie Savage scored against his father’s team as Reading eased into the second round with a 5-0 rout of Peterborough at the Weston Homes Stadium on Saturday.

This all-League One tie turned out to be one of the most one-sided of the day, with the Peterborough manager, Robbie Savage, watching on in disbelief as his side were pulled apart.

Reading went ahead after 26 minutes as slick passing led to Andy Rinomhota playing in Daniel Kyerewaa, who found the bottom corner via a deflection. Reading doubled their lead in the 34th minute when a cross from Haydon Roberts was met by a diving header from top scorer Jack Marriott.

It was in effect game over in first-half stoppage time as Savage deepened his father’s misery when he took possession after the ball ran off Marriott, his deflected effort finding the top corner.

Jamie Reid added a fourth for the visitors in the 72nd minute when Paudie O’Connor nodded Savage’s free-kick into his path for him to lift over the Peterborough goalkeeper Alex Bass. Reading struck yet again four minutes later when Liam Fraser’s pass put Reid clean through to score his second.

Non-league Kidderminster breezed into the second round with a convincing 3-0 victory over League One Doncaster.

The National League club opened the scoring after 22 minutes when Maz Kouhyar pulled the ball back to Lewis Walker, and he fired home at the second attempt after his initial shot had hit the upright.

The Harriers striker continued to cause problems, putting an effort over the bar and another just wide, but in the 36th minute he turned provider, charging upfield before teeing up Kouhyar and the on-loan Notts County midfielder slotted home. Kouhyar was again involved in the third goal, having a shot that Josh Clarke could only parry and David Davis turned in the rebound.

The Kidderminster manager, Paul Wotton, said: “We started well, scored the goal and got the crowd up. It was just a really good day. They are a League One team at the end of the day, no matter what the scoreline suggests. They are two leagues higher than us, so they are going to have moments in the game, but we stood up to it.”

League Two Exeter pulled off an upset with a 2-1 win away to League One leaders Huddersfield. Exeter took the lead after 12 minutes, thanks to a perfectly delivered cross from the left from Luca Woodhouse, with centre-back Jack Taylor stealing in at the far post to finish it off.

Huddersfield looked a different team in the second half and found an equaliser within eight minutes of the restart as Ibane Bowat headed home Cameron Humphreys’ corner at the back post.

Charlie Cummins grabbed the winner nine minutes from time at the end of a well-worked move up the right, culminating in Reece Cole’s cutback and a good finish.

Altrincham were denied another famous FA Cup upset as they conceded an 84-minute equaliser against Notts County before bowing out in a penalty shootout.

County took the lead through Jacob Bedeau in the 28th minute but Altrincham responded well with Lucas Weaver grabbing an equaliser six minutes before half-time. Lewis Banks gave the hosts the lead just before the hour but Callum Roberts dashed Altrincham’s hopes of another cup scalp, having beaten 17 Football League sides in the competition, scoring with a first-time strike to force extra-time.

With neither side able to make a breakthrough in extra-time the game went to penalties and Aidan Barlow, Sam Taylor and Eddy Jones all missed from the spot for Altrincham as County triumphed 3-2.

Blackpool survived a scare at Hornchurch, needing to rely on a 118th-minute winner from Josh Bowler to secure a 2-1 comeback victory at the Hornchurch Stadium.

Fleetwood’s hopes of following up their memorable Carabao Cup upset against Premier League champions Arsenal with a long FA Cup run are over after a 2-1 home defeat by fellow League Two side Rochdale. Baba Adeeko’s goal in extra time at Highbury sent the visitors through.

Chesterfield withstood a second-half comeback from Yeovil Town to secure their place in the second round with a 4-3 victory. Yeovil recovered from 3-1 down to level at 3-3 before Joel Randall struck the winner for the Spireites a minute from time.

Late Mansfield goals from Rhys Oates and Jordan Bowery ended the plucky Cup resistance of National League North Macclesfield. Nathan Moriah-Welsh gave Mansfield a first-half lead but the Silkmen were still in the tie under Oates made it 2-0 in the 72nd minute. Bowery added a third three minutes into added time to wrap up victory for the Stags.

League One Plymouth eased through thanks to three goals in a late 11-minute spell in a 4-0 win against Southern League Premier Central battlers Alvechurch. Will Evans finally broke the deadlock after 50 minutes, winning the ball from Jessy Bavanganga before driving a low angled shot into the far corner. Further goals from Evans, Michael Baidoo and Ronan Curtis saw the Pilgrims through.

League One strugglers Barnsley booked their spot in the second round with a 7-2 win over Aldershot at Oakwell, with Cameron McGeehan grabbing a hat-trick.

Leyton Orient held off Harborough 5-1 to progress into the second round while League Two high-flyers Crewe beat Wimbledon 2-1.

Nick Powell and Adam Phillips scored twice as Bradford thrashed National League North side Marine 7-0, while a late goal from Joel Randall helped Cheltenham close out a dramatic 4-3 win over National League Yeovil.

Last season’s quarter-finalists Port Vale booked their place in the second round with a 4-2 victory over National League strugglers Scunthorpe United at Vale Park. MK Dons avoided an upset as they ground out a 2-1 win over League Two Swindon.

Southern League Premier Central team Worcester’s hopes of an upset were ended in a 1-0 defeat at League Two Colchester while Jack Bates scored twice in the first half as Dover progressed with a 2-0 win over Wealdstone.

Ollie Pearce scored after 10 seconds as York sealed a 4-0 win over Northampton. The City captain also bagged a second before Alex Hunt and Josh Stones completed the rout.

Jordan Thewlis’ stoppage-time penalty gave seventh-tier Guiseley a 1-0 win over Sutton at Nethermoor Park as Carlisle beat League Two leaders Salford 1-0. Ryan Graydon missed a penalty for the visitors before David Ajiboye’s goal just before the break proved enough to send the Cumbrians through.

Eighth-tier AFC Rushden + Diamonds slipped to a 4-0 defeat at Burton. Will Collar and Borges Rodrigues scored for the Brewers in the first half, with Charlie Webster and Zac Scutt adding two more late on.

Nathan Odokonyero scored twice as National League South Salisbury saw off seventh-tier Sholing 6-0 to take their place in round two for the first time since reforming in 2015.

#806. Scottish roundup: Flying Falkirk hit five to shatter Hearts’ long unbeaten home run

Falkirk leapfrog their hosts with 5-2 rout at Tynecastle

Liam Scales gives Celtic 1-0 home win over Kilmarnock

Rampant Falkirk obliterated Hearts’ 18-month unbeaten home record in the Scottish Premiership with a stunning 5-2 win at Tynecastle on Sunday as they leapfrogged their hosts into third place.

Wouter Vrancken’s beleaguered side, missing 11 players through injury, were in disarray as swashbuckling Falkirk romped into a five-goal lead early in the second half through Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double. Hearts hit back through the substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Cláudio Braga penalty, but Falkirk were well worthy of making it five top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1995.

A stunned Vrancken said: “This is an embarrassment, the first half for sure. It’s crazy, crazy, and everybody – me, staff, players – have to take responsibility in those things. This is ridiculous.”

It was a first league defeat at Tynecastle for Hearts since April 2025 and they have won just two of their past 11 matches. Falkirk move into third, a point above Hearts, although they have played a game more.

Liam Scales provided a looping finish to earn Celtic a 1-0 home victory over Kilmarnock later on Sunday. The Irish defender hooked a Camilo Durán cross into the top corner in the 26th minute to restore Celtic’s four-point lead at the top of the table.

Celtic – and Kasper Høgh in particular – otherwise had a frustrating day in front of goal, with Benjamin Nygren missing a second-half penalty. Høgh had an early goal disallowed as his barren run without a goal hit the 16-game mark since he netted a hat-trick at Kilmarnock on his second appearance. Celtic manager Martin O’Neill said: “I thought Kasper was off the mark for about 35 seconds. I think he would maybe have scored the next chance if the first had counted, but he worked really hard for us.”

Rangers banished their recent away day blues with a solid 2-0 win at St Mirren on Saturday.

Draws against Dundee and Hearts in their last two Scottish Premiership games away from Ibrox had blemished their title challenge, but Derek McInnes’s side were determined to leave Paisley without a mark on them.

The in-form striker Ryan Naderi scored with a soft penalty after 18 minutes before the returning skipper, Dan Neil, added a second just after the hour mark with a deflected strike to extend Rangers’ unbeaten run in all competitions to 12 games.

The Aberdeen manager, Stephen Robinson, insists he will face the challenge head on as his side go into the international break in real trouble at the wrong end of the table.

Hibernian started the evening three points behind Robinson’s side, but a dominant second-half performance in a 4-0 victory at Pittodrie allowed the Edinburgh club to overtake their hosts in 10th place on goal difference.

The hosts showed promise early in the game and the Hibs keeper Raphael Sallinger saved well from Jack Milne, who also hit the bar for Aberdeen before Jamie McGrath’s 25-yard strike found the target. Aberdeen went all-out in search of an equaliser, but quickly fell 2-0 behind to Callum Wright, sparking calls for Robinson’s head from the home support. Further strikes from Thibault Klidjé and Nicky Cadden completed the rout.

Robinson said: “It’s really, really disappointing, there’s no hiding away from it. It was an unacceptable performance and an unacceptable result. We haven’t taken our chances – Hibs had five or six chances and took four of them – [and] that’s always the difference in football. We got the result we deserved.

“It’s a difficult situation, difficult for myself, the players and the club. I will keep fighting until told otherwise. We have to be better than that, that’s not acceptable. We have to get players who want to fight and try to get us out of this situation.”

Jim Goodwin, the home manager, hit out at the decision to award the penalty that cost Dundee United dear in a 1-1 draw against Motherwell at Tannadice.

The referee, Ryan Lee, had initially given a free-kick for offside in the early stages of the game. However, he was then advised by the VAR, Andrew Dallas, to have another look at an incident where Tawanda Maswanhise had gone down in the United box under a challenge by the home skipper, Dylan Tait. After checking the pitchside monitor, the referee pointed to the spot with the Motherwell captain, Lukas Fadinger, tucking the penalty away.

The hosts ultimately salvaged a point thanks to Jesse Randall’s goal but Goodwin insisted his side should have had all three. “It’s a poor decision for me,” he said. “I know it’s going to be subjective and people will have their own opinions on it, but I don’t know what Dylan Tait is meant to do.” Unsurprisingly, the Motherwell manager, Alfred Johansson, disagreed with Goodwin’s assessment, saying: “He’s on the ball and gets down from a tackle, and it’s a penalty.”

Simo Valakari was thrilled to give St Johnstone supporters a 2-1 victory over Dundee to celebrate after recent Perth struggles against their Tayside rivals.

Josh Campbell headed the home side in front after five minutes. The substitute Joe Westley replied early in the second half after a mix-up between the keeper Ross Sinclair and Cheick Diabate. Kai Fotheringham, on his first Premiership start for St Johnstone, netted a deflected winner on 72 minutes.

#805. Lifetime's Natasha Wilson Sues After "Disfigurement" From Dog Attack

Natasha Wilson—known for her role in Lifetime's UnREAL—filed a lawsuit against a dog owner after suffering what she described as facial "disfigurement" from a bite.

Natasha Wilson is seeking justice after a harrowing run-in with a dog.

In a lawsuit filed on Nov. 3 and obtained by E! News, the Lifetime star—who appeared in Single and Ready to Jingle, Trust in Love as well as the UnREAL series—said she has been unable to work in the two years since being bitten by a dog named Scruffy at a Los Angeles dog park.

She is suing the dog's owner Gregory Marcel, who she alleges did not have Scruffy on his leash and "could not promptly reach, control, or restrain the dog" when the animal approached her French bulldog on Nov. 7, 2024.

According to the complaint, Scruffy allegedly stood over Wilson's bulldog "in an aggressive and dominant posture" and jumped at the actress when she tried to intervene, knocking her to the ground.

Wilson then claimed that Scruffy continued to attack her while she was "on the ground attempting to shield her dog with her body and hands,” per the filing.

"During the attack, Scruffy bit [Wilson] on the face, above her right eyebrow," the lawsuit alleged. Upon seeking treatment at a local hospital, Wilson said she was diagnosed with a "facial laceration," prompting medical workers to irrigate and loosely suture her wound because of "the risk of infection associated with dog bites."

"As a result of the incident, [Wilson] suffered a laceration above her right eyebrow requiring sutures and has been left with a permanent, visible, and painful scar, an altered eyebrow hair pattern, hypersensitivity at the site of the wound, and impaired movement of the right brow," the suit read, alleging that she has also been "advised that she requires scar revision surgery and additional treatment."

Wilson said she now has permanent scarring above her right eyebrow as well as "shock and injury to her nervous system, all of which have caused "great physical, mental, and nervous pain and suffering, disfigurement, and emotional distress."

"As a further direct and proximate result of the bite, [Wilson] was prevented from attending to her usual occupation," the complaint added, "and thereby sustained a loss of earnings and an impairment of her earning capacity."

Wilson is suing Marcel for damages, including medical expenses associated with her injury.

E! News has attempted to locate an attorney for Marcel for comment but was unable to do so.

#803. Diego Gómez hits another stunner as Brighton beat 10-man Brentford to go second

Who can stop Brighton’s ­ascension in English and European football? They are setting standards, ­practices ­leaving almost everybody else ­trailing in their wake. A ­second‑place position in the ­Premier League would once have read like a glitch in a ­Football ­Manager ­session. Not in November 2026, where they appear the only team capable of throwing down any sort of challenge to Arsenal.

Under low winter sun, Brentford, an opposition to which Brighton are often, if lazily, compared, were ­swatted aside. If Keith Andrews’s team, and their fans at the Amex ­Stadium, could level blame at a couple of ­refereeing decisions, they received little chance of rescuing anything. Brighton squeezed them, toyed with them.

If Pascal Gross, scorer of a perfectly hit penalty, attempted to dampen expectations of a title challenge, his manager, Fabian Hürzeler, allowed fans to dream. “They should always be excited, it’s our job to make them excited,” he said.

A successful return to the Amex Stadium following five Brighton away trips, more than 5,000 miles on the road including victories at ­Manchester City and Getafe over the past two outings. Brentford returned to a stadium where they have never won in the Premier League. Normal service was duly resumed, any Brighton negatives coming in a failure to add to their first-half goals.

An up-and-under straight from the kick-off was a rare Brentford foray into the Brighton box. Bart Verburggen catching it on the full prefaced an easy afternoon for the Brighton goalkeeper. There are many further dimensions to ­Hürzeler’s team. Last week Paul Scholes, an unlikely ­progressive, declared himself an admirer of a “level of ­coaching” he suggested is ­unsurpassed in ­English football. “The one thing that is non‑negotiable is to always put the team first,” Hürzeler said.

Diego Gómez’s opener was not as spectacular as the halfway-line goal of the season against Crystal Palace but a beauty nonetheless. Caressing the ball first with his left and then with his right, he laid up a thrash past Caoimhín Kelleher. Its trajectory was unerring, unstoppable. Hürzeler revealed: “Yesterday, he changed to shooting with [his] left foot … I couldn’t see him scoring with his left foot. I asked him after where this quality came from.”

The path to a commanding win opened up. Igor Thiago did not last many ­minutes beyond his failed attempt to lob ­Verburggen. Scuffling in midfield with Chema Andrés, his shove was first ruled a yellow by the referee, Michael Oliver. In stepped the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell: “violent conduct” and “with force” was the verdict from Stockley Park.

Afterwards, Andrews was ­visibly unhappy: “We’ve lost two games and both when down to 10 men. So we need to analyse ourselves first. In both scenarios we can do better. In both scenarios the opposition player has been the one to provoke the situation.”

Infact, both Yehor Yarmolyuk and Vitaly Janelt were dismissed against Liverpool, and if Andrews rues such lapses of discipline he was more unhappy at the initial decision’s video-assisted overturn: “The game is in a state now of a place I don’t particularly like.”

Straying beyond the confines of his technical area in a manner likely to add him to Mikel Arteta’s “massive storage of images” of such breaches, Andrews asked his team to dig deep but Brighton’s dominance of possession became near-total.

Luka Vuskovic, ­serving ­previously as a deep-lying playmaker, won the penalty. Keane Lewis-Potter’s ­panicked response to a physical 18-yard box mismatch was to snatch at the ­Croatian’s shirt. Gross’s penalty was struck as truly as Gómez’s goal. “We need to be cuter,” Andrews said. “I take real pride in the way we defend set pieces and we need to do better because that wasn’t good.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andrews’s half-time ­adjustments, bringing on Yarmolyuk and Nathan Collins, was an attempt to protect Brentford’s goal difference. Brighton continued to pile on pressure, their ­possession share reaching beyond 75%. A set piece became Brentford’s sole route back, though Mathias Jensen’s diagonal into ­Verbruggen’s hands would not have passed muster in rugby’s Nations Championship.

Ironic cheers from the away end came when Brentford won a corner, and then another – rare excitement at Brighton’s defenders being asked to do something other than build an attack. The visitors’ fighting spirit at least sustained, though threatened to spill over. When Kevin Schade shoved ­Vuskovic to the ground by the touchline, another red card was a possibility, only for Oliver and Attwell to rule a yellow as sufficient this time.

Brighton’s push for honours and further horizons will require more than spectacular goals. “You see the Premier League, the margins, you look at the results – we are not ­getting carried away yet,” Gross said. “Every game we have to suffer a lot.”

Hürzeler, like Andrews constantly straying beyond the confines of his technical area, does not countenance any let-ups. When Brighton meet the unstinting demands of their coach, so many are left in their wing mirrors.

#802. The palaeo cave art that hid in plain sight for 26,000 years

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chris Simms is a science writer based in Somerset, UK.

Inscriptions at the Cova de la Font Major cave system in Catalonia in northeastern Spain prompts rethink of prehistoric population and cultural trends. Credit: Vergès Bosch, J. M., Salas-Altès, M./Antiquity

Inscriptions at the Cova de la Font Major cave system in Catalonia in northeastern Spain prompts rethink of prehistoric population and cultural trends. Credit: Vergès Bosch, J. M., Salas-Altès, M./Antiquity

Archaeologists have described hundreds of rock-art engravings dating back around 26,000 years in a cave frequently visited by tourists in Catalonia — a region of northeastern Spain that was thought to be almost devoid of palaeolithic art1. The findings were published in the journal Antiquity on 5 November.

Josep Maria Vergès Bosch, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) in Tarragona, Spain, spotted some prehistoric engravings among more-modern graffiti in the Cova de la Font Major during a planned excavation in 2019.

Vergès and archaeologist Míriam Salas-Altès at IPHES-CERCA studied 280 Palaeolithic art motifs, including 55 animal depictions, from the cave. “The sheer quantity of art discovered at the Cova de la Font Major is exceptional,” says Salas-Altès.

The cave system — made up of more than 3.5 kilometres of underground passageways that have been occupied numerous times during human history — has been open to the public for some seven decades and became a museum in the 1990s.

The drawings were easy to miss. “When you shine a light straight on the engravings, they are really difficult to see, you have to play with light from different directions to see the depressions,” says Salas-Altès.

Researcher Míriam Salas-Altès documents engravings in a tunnel of the cave system. Credit: Josep Maria Vergès/IPHES-CERCA

The etchings include images of animals such as a horse, a bear and an aurochs (the ancestor of domestic cattle), as well as myriad swirling lines. A handful of the engravings reveal how the artists used “natural lines or fissures in the walls”, says Salas-Altès. For example, “one is used to represent the ground under a horse”.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03585-z

Vergès Bosch, J. M. & Salas-Altès, M. Antiquity https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2026.10447 (2027).
